name: Korčula
tagline: A quieter, equally beautiful alternative to Hvar, a walled medieval town on a herringbone street plan that claims Marco Polo as a native son.
highlight: Wandering the old town's herringbone streets, each angled just enough to block the wind and let the sea breeze cool every doorway.
shortDescription: A quieter, equally beautiful alternative to Hvar, a walled medieval town that claims Marco Polo as a native son, surrounded by Korčula's own vineyards.
metaDescription: A Korčula travel guide: St Mark's Cathedral, Marco Polo's birthplace, the old town walls, Pošip wine, food and how to plan a Dalmatian island trip.
nearestAirport: Dubrovnik Airport (DBV), about 2.5 hours by road and ferry
knownFor: St Mark's Cathedral, Marco Polo's alleged birthplace, Pošip wine

image.alt: Korčula's walled old town on its peninsula

intro: Korčula is a quieter, equally beautiful alternative to Hvar, a walled medieval town on its own small peninsula off Croatia's Pelješac Peninsula.
Its old town is famous for a clever herringbone street plan, angled to funnel cooling sea breezes through the main streets while blocking the harsher winter winds.
The island also claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo, and produces some of Croatia's most respected white wine from vineyards right outside the old town walls.

whyVisit.intro: Korčula's case rests on Dalmatian island beauty without Hvar's crowds or price tag.

points.title: The old town is a walled medieval showpiece
points.text: A compact, herringbone-planned peninsula town rivalling Dubrovnik's architecture on a smaller scale.

points.title: It's quieter and more affordable than Hvar
points.text: A similar Dalmatian island experience with noticeably fewer crowds.

points.title: The Marco Polo connection is a fun draw
points.text: Local legend places the explorer's birthplace right in the old town.

points.title: The wine is excellent
points.text: Pošip, a distinctive white grape, is grown almost exclusively on this island.

points.title: It works well paired with Hvar or Dubrovnik
points.text: An easy ferry connection makes it a natural island-hopping addition.

attractionsIntro: Korčula's essential sights are concentrated within its compact, walled old town.

attractions.name: Korčula's old town peninsula

image.alt: Korčula's old town on its peninsula

attractions.text: A walled medieval town on its own small peninsula, its fortifications still substantially intact.
attractions.tip: Walk the perimeter path for the best views of the walls from outside.

attractions.name: St Mark's Cathedral
attractions.text: The old town's centrepiece, a Gothic-Renaissance cathedral built from local stone on the main square.
attractions.tip: Look for the carvings by Korčula's own stonemasons, renowned across Dalmatia.

attractions.name: St Mark's Square and the Venetian Governor's Palace

image.file: File:Korcula, main square, cathedral St. Mark, Venetian governor's palace.jpg

attractions.text: The old town's civic heart, ringed by the cathedral, bishop's palace and former Venetian governor's residence.
attractions.tip: A lovely spot for an evening coffee once the day-trip crowds have thinned.

attractions.name: Marco Polo's alleged birthplace

image.alt: The house said to be Marco Polo's birthplace in Korčula

attractions.text: A beloved local legend, a modest stone house said to be where the famous explorer was born in 1254.
attractions.tip: Treat the connection as charming folklore rather than settled historical fact — scholars dispute it.

attractions.name: St Mark's Cathedral's interior

image.alt: The interior of St Mark's Cathedral in Korčula

attractions.text: Worth a proper look inside, featuring works attributed to Venetian master Tintoretto.
attractions.tip: Combine with the adjacent Treasury and Bishop's Palace museums for the fuller story.

attractions.name: St Peter's Church

image.file: File:Korcula, St. Peter's Church and alleged Marco Polo birth house (left).png
image.alt: St Peter's Church near Marco Polo's alleged birthplace in Korčula

attractions.text: A modest but atmospheric church right beside the Marco Polo house, part of the same historic corner.
attractions.tip: An easy stop combined with the Marco Polo house next door.

attractions.name: The old town walls from the water

image.alt: Korčula's old town walls seen from the water

attractions.text: A striking sight, the old town's fortified silhouette rising directly from the sea.
attractions.tip: A short boat trip or ferry arrival both offer this classic view.

thingsToDoIntro: Korčula rewards a slow pace, best spent wandering the old town and tasting the island's own wine.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the old town's herringbone streets
thingsToDo.text: A fascinating piece of town planning, streets deliberately angled to channel sea breezes and block winter winds.
thingsToDo.tip: Compare the straight main street to the curved side streets to see the clever design in action.

thingsToDo.title: Tour Marco Polo's alleged birthplace

image.file: File:Birthplace of Marco Polo, Korcula, Croatia.JPG
image.alt: The house said to be Marco Polo's birthplace

thingsToDo.text: A fun, low-key stop, climbing the modest house's tower for a view over the old town's rooftops.
thingsToDo.tip: Don't expect much in the way of historical artefacts — this is more atmosphere than museum.

thingsToDo.title: Explore St Mark's Cathedral

image.file: File:INTERIOR ST. MARK'S CATHEDRAL, KORCULA, CROATIA.jpg
image.alt: The interior of St Mark's Cathedral in Korčula

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile visit, taking in the cathedral's carved stonework and Venetian-era artwork.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with the Bishop's Treasury next door for a fuller sense of the island's history.

thingsToDo.title: Watch a Moreška sword dance performance
thingsToDo.text: A unique local tradition, a centuries-old choreographed sword dance performed in the old town in summer.
thingsToDo.tip: Check performance schedules ahead — shows typically run on a set evening each week in season.

thingsToDo.title: Swim at a beach outside the walls
thingsToDo.text: An easy way to cool off, small pebble beaches dotted around the peninsula just outside the old town.
thingsToDo.tip: Rent a kayak or paddleboard for a closer look at the walls from the water.

thingsToDo.title: Photograph the old town from the water

image.alt: Korčula's old town photographed from the water

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding pursuit, the walled peninsula town photographing beautifully from nearly any angle offshore.
thingsToDo.tip: Golden hour light works especially well on the old town's pale stone walls.

foodIntro: Korčula's food centres on its own respected white wine alongside classic Dalmatian cooking.

foods.name: Pošip wine

image.alt: Pošip, a white wine grown almost exclusively on Korčula

foods.text: One of Croatia's most respected white wines, a grape grown almost exclusively on this island.
foods.whereToTry: Wine bars throughout the old town, or wineries a short drive inland.

foods.name: Žrnovski makaruni
foods.text: A distinctive local pasta, hand-rolled in the nearby village of Žrnovo and traditionally served with a rich meat sauce.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional konobas, especially those specialising in Korčula home cooking.

foods.name: Fresh grilled seafood

image.alt: Grilled seafood at a traditional Croatian konoba

foods.text: A highlight of dining here, fish and shellfish grilled simply at old town konobas.

foods.name: Dalmatinski pršut (dry-cured ham)
foods.text: A reliable starter, often served with local cheese and olives.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants and konobas throughout the old town.

foods.name: Crni rižot (black risotto)

image.alt: Black risotto made with cuttlefish ink

foods.text: A Dalmatian classic, worth trying at least once during a Korčula visit.
foods.whereToTry: Seafood restaurants throughout the old town.

foods.name: Fritule (small fried doughnuts)
foods.text: A nice sweet treat, found at bakeries around the old town.

bestTime.headline: May, June and September for warm weather without peak crowds
bestTime.summary: Korčula is busiest in July and August, with shoulder months offering a quieter, better-value alternative.

seasons.text: Warm enough to swim, with noticeably thinner crowds than peak summer.
Warm and lively, though still noticeably calmer than Hvar at the same time of year.
Still warm enough for the sea, with crowds and prices both easing off.
Very quiet, with much of the island's hospitality scene closed for the season.

bestTime.avoid: Deep winter, when most restaurants and hotels close until spring.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Korčula visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Book ferry tickets ahead for peak summer sailings from Dubrovnik or Split.
Try Pošip wine at a local winery, not just a restaurant list.
Check for a Moreška sword dance performance during your visit.
Wear comfortable shoes — the old town's streets are cobbled and can be slippery.
Escape to Lumbarda's beaches when the old town feels busy with day-trippers.
Consider Korčula as a quieter alternative base to Hvar for a Dalmatian island stay.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Korčula?
faq.a: Two days covers the old town and a taste of the island's wine country comfortably.

faq.q: How do you get to Korčula?
faq.a: By catamaran from Dubrovnik or ferry from Split, or by car via the Pelješac Peninsula's car ferry.

faq.q: Was Marco Polo really born in Korčula?
faq.a: It's disputed by historians, though the local legend and the house said to be his birthplace remain a beloved part of the island's identity.

faq.q: How does Korčula compare to Hvar?
faq.a: Quieter and more affordable, offering a similar Dalmatian island experience with noticeably fewer crowds.

faq.q: Is Korčula good for wine lovers?
faq.a: Yes — Pošip, one of Croatia's best white wines, is grown almost exclusively on this island.

faq.q: Can you combine Korčula with Dubrovnik or Hvar?
faq.a: Yes, easily — ferry connections make it a natural addition to either destination.
